patient_information: A 51-year-old female Swiss traveller with no reported chronic underlying diseases and no regular intake of any medication.
chief_complaint: Generalized pruritic rash, conjunctivitis, and peripheral edema, with symptom onset two days prior to presentation.
history_of_present_illness: Four days after returning from her trip, the patient developed a generalized, slightly pruritic maculopapular rash on her face, trunk, and extremities. She was afebrile. The following day, the rash worsened, and she developed a non-purulent bilateral conjunctivitis. At the time of presentation, she also had tender edema of the hands, elbows, knees, and feet, along with generalized lymphadenopathy.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient presented six days after returning from a 2-week holiday to Guatemala and El Salvador. The clinical presentation and incubation period were consistent with arboviral infections which are prevalent in Central and South America.
physical_exam: Physical examination revealed a non-purulent bilateral conjunctivitis and a generalized maculopapular rash involving the face. There was tender edema of the hands, elbows, knees, and feet, as well as generalized lymphadenopathy affecting the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions.
labs_and_diagnostics: The full blood count and liver function tests were normal. C-reactive protein was 8 mg/L, and creatinine was mildly elevated at 87 μmol/L. Rapid diagnostic tests for dengue and chikungunya were negative. Blood samples sent to a reference laboratory confirmed Zika virus. The first serum sample, obtained 6 days after symptom onset, was positive for Zika RT-PCR. A second serum sample obtained 7 days later showed seroconversion, with Zika IgM IIFT becoming positive at 1:640 and Zika IgG IIFT rising from 1:20 to 1:5120. A rise in Dengue IgG IIFT to 1:5120 was interpreted as cross-reactivity.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis primarily included arboviral infections common in Central America, specifically dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. These infections can be clinically indistinguishable; however, the combination of a skin rash, conjunctivitis, and peripheral edema in an afebrile patient was considered highly suggestive of a Zika virus infection.
management_and_clinical_course: Rapid diagnostic tests for dengue and chikungunya were negative. Blood samples were sent to a reference laboratory for further testing, which confirmed the clinical suspicion of Zika virus. As arboviral infections are self-limiting and lack specific treatment, clinical management is exclusively supportive.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is Zika virus infection. This was confirmed based on laboratory results which included a positive Zika RT-PCR on the initial blood sample and documented seroconversion on paired sera, with a negative to positive result for Zika IgM (1:640) and a significant fourfold rise in Zika IgG antibody titres (1:20 to 1:5120). The rise in anti-Dengue IgG was considered to be due to cross-reactivity.
